original.title: Two springs: calibration from an energy measurement
original.stem_html: Two fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) on a smooth horizontal table are \(3\,\mathrm m\) apart. A particle of mass \(1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\) is connected to \(A\) by a light spring of natural length \(1.2\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(\lambda\,\mathrm N\), and to \(B\) by a second light spring of natural length \(0.8\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(\frac23\lambda\,\mathrm N\). The springs and particle lie along \(AB\). Let \(E\) be the equilibrium position. Both springs obey Hooke's law in extension and compression.
original.question_html:
Two fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) on a smooth horizontal table are \(3\,\mathrm m\) apart. A particle of mass \(1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\) is connected to \(A\) by a light spring of natural length \(1.2\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(\lambda\,\mathrm N\), and to \(B\) by a second light spring of natural length \(0.8\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(\frac23\lambda\,\mathrm N\). The springs and particle lie along \(AB\). Let \(E\) be the equilibrium position. Both springs obey Hooke's law in extension and compression.

(a) [3]

Find \(AE\), and express the common spring tension at \(E\) in terms of \(\lambda\).

(b) [4]

The particle is displaced \(0.2\,\mathrm m\) from \(E\) towards \(B\) and released from rest. Its speed at \(E\) is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find \(\lambda\), using energy.

(c) [3]

For the same motion, find the speed and the resultant force when the particle is \(0.12\,\mathrm m\) from \(E\) towards \(A\).

(d) [2]

In a separate trial the particle is projected from \(E\). Find the greatest launch speed for which neither spring is compressed.
original.hint_html: First compare the stiffnesses \(\lambda/l\). For the dynamics, subtract the elastic energy at equilibrium.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(AE=1.7\,\mathrm m\); common tension \(=5\lambda/12\,\mathrm N\).

(b)

\(\lambda=90\).

(c)

Speed \(1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); force \(18\,\mathrm N\) towards \(E\).

(d)

\(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The stiffnesses are equal: \[k_A=\frac{\lambda}{1.2}=\frac{5\lambda}{6},\qquad k_B=\frac{(2/3)\lambda}{0.8}=\frac{5\lambda}{6}.\] Writing \(AE=s\), the extensions are \(s-1.2\) and \(2.2-s\). Equal tensions therefore give \(s-1.2=2.2-s\), so \(s=1.7\). Each extension is \(0.5\,\mathrm m\); hence each tension is \((5\lambda/6)(0.5)=5\lambda/12\,\mathrm N\).

Part (b)

For a displacement \(x\) towards \(B\), the extensions are \(0.5+x\) and \(0.5-x\). The increase in their total elastic energy above its value at \(E\) is \[\Delta U=\frac12\frac{5\lambda}{6}\big((0.5+x)^2+(0.5-x)^2-2(0.5)^2\big)=\frac{5\lambda}{6}x^2.\] At release this is \(\lambda/30\,\mathrm J\). It becomes kinetic energy at \(E\), so \[\frac{\lambda}{30}=\frac12(1.5)(2^2)=3.\] Thus \(\lambda=90\). Energy already stored at equilibrium is not all available for motion; only the energy difference is used.

Part (c)

Now each stiffness is \(75\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), and energy gives \[\frac12(1.5)v^2+75x^2=3.\] At \(x=-0.12\), \(v^2=4-100(0.12)^2=2.56\), so \(v=1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The signed resultant is \(75(0.5-x)-75(0.5+x)=-150x\). At \(x=-0.12\) this is \(+18\,\mathrm N\), towards \(B\), hence towards \(E\).

Part (d)

Neither spring is compressed precisely when \(|x|\leq0.5\). At a limiting turning point, \[\frac12(1.5)u^2=75(0.5)^2.\] Thus \(u^2=25\) and the greatest speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Equality is allowed: a spring may just reach natural length without compression.

original.title: Two strings with alternating slack phases
original.stem_html: Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are \(5a\) apart on a smooth horizontal table, where \(a\gt0\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is constrained by a smooth straight guide to move along \(AB\). It is joined to \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(mg\), and to \(B\) by another of natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(2mg\). Each string is slack when shorter than its natural length. The particle is held at \(AP=a/2\) and released from rest.
original.question_html:
Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are \(5a\) apart on a smooth horizontal table, where \(a\gt0\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is constrained by a smooth straight guide to move along \(AB\). It is joined to \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(mg\), and to \(B\) by another of natural length \(2a\) and modulus \(2mg\). Each string is slack when shorter than its natural length. The particle is held at \(AP=a/2\) and released from rest.

(a) [3]

Find the equilibrium position between \(A\) and \(B\), and the two tensions there.

(b) [3]

Find the speed when \(AP=a\) for the first time.

(c) [4]

While both strings are taut, put \(z=AP/a\). Obtain an expression for \(v^2\), and find the greatest speed during the motion.

(d) [4]

Find \(AP\) when \(P\) next comes to rest. Explain why the both-taut formula must not be used up to this point.
original.hint_html: The stiffnesses are equal, but the natural lengths are not. Split the motion at \(AP=a\) and \(AP=3a\).
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(AP=2a\); both tensions are \(mg\).

(b)

\(\frac32\sqrt{ag}\).

(c)

\(v^2=ag\big(\frac{17}{4}-2(z-2)^2\big)\); greatest speed \(\frac{\sqrt{17}}2\sqrt{ag}\).

(d)

\(AP=7a/2\); the right string is slack after \(AP=3a\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Both strings have stiffness \(mg/a\). When both are stretched and \(AP=s\), their extensions are \(s-a\) and \(3a-s\). Force balance requires \(s-a=3a-s\), giving \(s=2a\). Both extensions are \(a\), so each tension is \(mg\). This position lies in the both-taut interval \(a\lt s\lt3a\).

Part (b)

Initially the left string is slack. The right string has extension \(5a-a/2-2a=5a/2\). Thus the initial energy is \[U_0=\frac{mg}{2a}\left(\frac{5a}{2}\right)^2=\frac{25}{8}mga.\] At \(AP=a\), the right extension is \(2a\) and the left elastic energy is still zero. Hence \[\frac12mv^2=\frac{25}{8}mga-2mga=\frac98mga,\] so \(v=\frac32\sqrt{ag}\).

Part (c)

For \(1\leq z\leq3\), \[U=\frac12mga\big((z-1)^2+(3-z)^2\big)=mga\big((z-2)^2+1\big).\] Subtracting from \(U_0=25mga/8\) gives the stated speed formula. The energy is least at \(z=2\), so the speed there is \(\sqrt{17ag}/2\).

Before \(z=1\), only the right string pulls the particle towards \(B\), and its speed increases. After \(z=3\), only the left string acts and its speed decreases. Therefore this is the greatest speed over the whole excursion, not just over the both-taut interval.

Part (d)

At \(z=3\), the speed is still \(3\sqrt{ag}/2\), so the particle continues beyond that point. The right string then becomes slack; it cannot store compression energy. The left string alone stores energy at the turning point: \[\frac{mg}{2a}(s-a)^2=\frac{25}{8}mga.\] Since \(s\gt3a\), take \(s-a=5a/2\), giving \(s=7a/2\). The kinetic energy is positive up to this point and the left tension opposes the motion, so this is the next stop. It lies before \(B\).

original.stem_html: Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are \(15a\) apart, with \(A\) vertically above \(B\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(km\), where \(k\gt0\), lies on the vertical line between them. It is joined to \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(3a\) and modulus \(6mg\), and to \(B\) by another of natural length \(5a\) and modulus \(5mg\).
original.question_html:
Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are \(15a\) apart, with \(A\) vertically above \(B\). A particle \(P\) of mass \(km\), where \(k\gt0\), lies on the vertical line between them. It is joined to \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(3a\) and modulus \(6mg\), and to \(B\) by another of natural length \(5a\) and modulus \(5mg\).

(a) [3]

Find \(BP\) in equilibrium when both strings are stretched, and state the range of \(k\) for which this is possible.

(b) [4]

The particle is held at \(BP=12a\) and released from rest. It next stops at \(BP=5a\). Find \(k\).
original.hint_html: The upper string pulls upwards, while the lower string and the weight act downwards. The two endpoints are natural-length boundaries.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(BP=za\). The upper extension is \((12-z)a\), giving tension \(2mg(12-z)\); the lower extension is \((z-5)a\), giving tension \(mg(z-5)\). Force balance gives \[2(12-z)-(z-5)-k=0,\] so \(z=(29-k)/3\). Both strings are stretched when \(5\lt z\lt12\). Combining this with \(k\gt0\) gives \(0\lt k\lt14\).

Part (b)

Initially the upper string is at natural length and the lower extension is \(7a\), so the elastic energy is \(49mga/2\). At the final point the lower string is at natural length and the upper extension is \(7a\), so the elastic energy is \(49mga\). The gravitational potential energy decreases by \(7kmga\). Thus \[\frac{49}{2}+7k=49,\] which gives \(k=7/2\).

For this value, the kinetic energy at an intermediate height is \[K=\frac32mga(12-z)(z-5).\] It is positive for \(5\lt z\lt12\), so no earlier stop occurs. Both strings are stretched throughout that open interval.

original.title: A midpoint attachment moving across a table
original.stem_html: A uniform light elastic string of natural length \(6a\) and modulus \(6mg\) has its ends fixed at points \(A\) and \(B\), \(8a\) apart on a smooth horizontal table. A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its midpoint. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). Initially the particle is held off the line \(AB\), with \(AP=BP=L\), then released. It moves along the perpendicular bisector and passes through \(M\) with speed \(\sqrt{12ag}\).
original.question_html:
A uniform light elastic string of natural length \(6a\) and modulus \(6mg\) has its ends fixed at points \(A\) and \(B\), \(8a\) apart on a smooth horizontal table. A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its midpoint. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). Initially the particle is held off the line \(AB\), with \(AP=BP=L\), then released. It moves along the perpendicular bisector and passes through \(M\) with speed \(\sqrt{12ag}\).

(a) [4]

Find \(L\).

(b) [2]

Find the initial acceleration.

(c) [2]

Find the tension in each half-string at \(M\), and explain why the resultant horizontal force is zero there despite the non-zero tensions.
original.hint_html: The string is still stretched at the midpoint between the fixed ends. Each half keeps the original modulus.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(L=5a\).

(b)

\(24g/5\), towards \(M\).

(c)

Each tension is \(2mg\); the forces are equal and opposite along \(AB\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Each half-string has natural length \(3a\), modulus \(6mg\), and stiffness \(2mg/a\). The total elastic energy at a half-length \(l\) is therefore \[2\frac{6mg}{2(3a)}(l-3a)^2=\frac{2mg}{a}(l-3a)^2.\] At \(M\), each length is \(4a\), so elastic energy remains \(2mga\); it is not zero. Conservation of energy gives \[\frac{2mg}{a}(L-3a)^2-2mga=\frac12m(12ag)=6mga.\] Thus \((L-3a)^2=4a^2\). Geometry requires \(L\geq4a\), so \(L=5a\), not \(a\).

Part (b)

Initially \(MP=\sqrt{(5a)^2-(4a)^2}=3a\). Each tension is \((2mg/a)(2a)=4mg\). Its component towards \(M\) is \(4mg(3/5)\). The two such components add, so the acceleration is \(2(4mg)(3/5)/m=24g/5\), towards \(M\).

Part (c)

At \(M\), each extension is \(a\), so each tension is \(2mg\). The two string segments lie on the same straight line, on opposite sides of the particle. Their force vectors cancel even though each half is stretched and stores elastic energy. Zero resultant does not mean zero tension.

original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(4mg\). It moves steadily in a non-degenerate horizontal circle, with the string at \(60^\circ\) to the downward vertical. In all trials the maximum permitted tension is \(3mg\).
original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(4mg\). It moves steadily in a non-degenerate horizontal circle, with the string at \(60^\circ\) to the downward vertical. In all trials the maximum permitted tension is \(3mg\).

(a) [4]

Find the stretched length of the string, the radius of the circle and the speed of the particle.

(b) [4]

For the same particle and string, find the range of possible values of \(\omega^2\) for steady non-degenerate circles respecting the tension limit.

(c) [4]

(a)

Length \(3a/2\), radius \(3\sqrt3a/4\), speed \(3\sqrt{ag}/2\).

(b)

original.stem_html: A light spring of natural length \(1\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(75\,\mathrm N\) is suspended vertically from a fixed point \(O\). A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), together with an additional load of mass \(M\,\mathrm{kg}\), hangs at rest from its lower end. original.question_html:
A light spring of natural length \(1\,\mathrm m\) and modulus \(75\,\mathrm N\) is suspended vertically from a fixed point \(O\). A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), together with an additional load of mass \(M\,\mathrm{kg}\), hangs at rest from its lower end. The additional load is removed without giving the remaining particle an impulse. During its first upward motion, the particle has speed \(0.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at a distance \(1.52\,\mathrm m\) below \(O\). Use \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

(a) [4]

Find the new equilibrium length. Let \(q\) be downward displacement from that equilibrium and \(D\) its value immediately after removal. Show by energy that \(\frac32v^2+\frac{75}{2}q^2=\frac{75}{2}D^2\).

(b) [4]

Find \(D\) and the removed mass \(M\).

(c) [3]

Find the least distance below \(O\) reached by the particle, and the least tension during the motion.

(d) [3]

Would replacing the spring by an elastic string with the same natural length and modulus alter this motion? Give a reasoned answer.
original.hint_html: Use the new equilibrium as the energy reference, but use the old equilibrium to determine the mass that was removed.
original.answer_html:
(a)

New equilibrium length \(1.4\,\mathrm m\); the stated energy relation follows.

(b)

\(D=0.2\,\mathrm m\), \(M=1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

(c)

Least distance \(1.2\,\mathrm m\); least tension \(15\,\mathrm N\).

(d)

No, in the stated ideal model: the length remains between \(1.2\) and \(1.6\,\mathrm m\), so the string would always be stretched.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The stiffness is \(75\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\). After removal, equilibrium requires \(75e_0=30\), so \(e_0=0.4\,\mathrm m\) and the equilibrium length is \(1.4\,\mathrm m\).

At downward displacement \(q\), the change of total potential energy from its equilibrium value is \[\frac{75}{2}\big((0.4+q)^2-0.4^2\big)-30q=\frac{75}{2}q^2.\] The linear terms cancel because the reference position is equilibrium. Initially \(q=D\) and the speed is zero, so conservation of energy gives the required equation.

Part (b)

At the specified point, \(q=1.52-1.4=0.12\). Substitution gives \[D^2=0.12^2+\frac{3}{75}(0.8)^2=0.0144+0.0256=0.04.\] The old equilibrium was lower, so \(D=0.2\,\mathrm m\). The extra extension \(D\) supported the extra weight: \(75D=10M\). Therefore \(M=1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

Part (c)

At either turning point, \(v=0\), so \(q=\pm D\). The upper point has \(q=-0.2\), giving length \(1.4-0.2=1.2\,\mathrm m\). Its extension is \(0.2\,\mathrm m\), so the tension there is \(75(0.2)=15\,\mathrm N\). This is the least tension because the extension is least there.

Part (d)

The lower turning length is the initial length \(1.4+0.2=1.6\,\mathrm m\), and the upper turning length is \(1.2\,\mathrm m\). Throughout the motion the length exceeds \(1\,\mathrm m\). Therefore a replacement string never becomes slack and exerts exactly the same force as the spring at every position. The force law, initial position and initial speed are identical, so the predicted motion is identical. The conclusion would not be valid for a motion involving spring compression.

original.title: A change of mass: compression or a slack phase?
original.stem_html: A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(kmg\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) on a smooth plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\alpha=3/5\). A particle of mass \(5m\) hangs down the line of greatest slope from \(O\), in equilibrium with spring length \(3a/2\). It is replaced by a particle of mass \(m\), held at the same position and then released from rest. The spring is constrained to remain straight and obeys Hooke's law in extension and compression.
original.question_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(kmg\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) on a smooth plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\alpha=3/5\). A particle of mass \(5m\) hangs down the line of greatest slope from \(O\), in equilibrium with spring length \(3a/2\). It is replaced by a particle of mass \(m\), held at the same position and then released from rest. The spring is constrained to remain straight and obeys Hooke's law in extension and compression.

(a) [3]

Find \(k\) and the new equilibrium length.

(b) [5]

Use energy to find the greatest speed of the new particle and its distance from \(O\) when it next comes to rest.

(c) [3]

Find the greatest magnitude of the spring force and the greatest magnitude of the acceleration during the motion.

(d) [3]

In a separate trial replace the spring by an elastic string with the same natural length and modulus, keeping the release position unchanged. Find the distance from \(O\) at the next stop.
original.hint_html: Energy about the new equilibrium is quadratic, but that formula remains valid through compression only for a spring.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=6\); new equilibrium length \(11a/10\).

(b)

Greatest speed \(\frac{2\sqrt6}{5}\sqrt{ag}\); next resting position \(OP=7a/10\).

(c)

Greatest spring-force magnitude \(3mg\); greatest acceleration magnitude \(12g/5\).

(d)

\(OP=a/4\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Initially the tension is \(5mg(3/5)=3mg\). Since the extension is \(a/2\), Hooke's law gives \(kmg/2=3mg\), so \(k=6\). For the new particle, equilibrium requires \[\frac{6mg}{a}e_0=\frac35mg,\] so \(e_0=a/10\) and the new equilibrium length is \(11a/10\).

Part (b)

Let \(s=OP\) and let \(x=s-11a/10\). The total potential energy differs from its equilibrium value by \(3mgx^2/a\): the linear elastic term cancels the gravitational term. At release \(x=2a/5\). Thus \[\frac12mv^2+\frac{3mg}{a}x^2=\frac{3mg}{a}\left(\frac{2a}{5}\right)^2.\] The greatest speed occurs at \(x=0\), giving \(v^2=24ag/25\). At the next stop \(x=-2a/5\), so \(s=11a/10-2a/5=7a/10\). The spring is compressed by \(3a/10\) there, which is permitted for the stated spring model.

Part (c)

The signed extension ranges from \(-3a/10\) to \(a/2\). Therefore the largest absolute extension is \(a/2\), giving a spring-force magnitude \(3mg\).

The resultant along the plane is \(-6mgx/a\), so acceleration has magnitude \(6g|x|/a\). Its largest value is \(6g(2a/5)/a=12g/5\). The spring force alone is not the resultant; the component of weight must be included.

Part (d)

Until the length reaches \(a\), the force is unchanged. At \(s=a\), \(x=-a/10\), and the energy equation gives \(v^2=9ag/10\). The string is then slack. The particle continues up the plane with constant deceleration \(3g/5\), and travels a further distance \[d=\frac{9ag/10}{2(3g/5)}=\frac{3a}{4}.\] Thus the next stop is at \(OP=a-d=a/4\), before the particle reaches the attachment point. Compression energy must not be assigned to the slack string.

original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(3M\) hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(8Mg\). original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(3M\) hangs in equilibrium from a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(8Mg\). A second particle of mass \(M\) is attached while the original particle is held fixed; the combined particle is then released from rest. No impulse or energy from an impact is involved.

(a) [4]

(b) [2]

original.hint_html: The additional mass changes the weight, but the extension cannot jump when it is attached.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The original equilibrium extension satisfies \(8Mg e_0/a=3Mg\), so \(e_0=3a/8\). After the specified descent it is \(a/2\). The new mass is \(4M\). The gravitational-energy loss is \(4Mg(a/8)=Mga/2\), while the elastic-energy increase is \[\frac{4Mg}{a}\left(\frac{a^2}{4}-\frac{9a^2}{64}\right)=\frac7{16}Mga.\] Hence \(\frac12(4M)v^2=Mga/16\), so \(v^2=ag/32\).

Part (b)

The new equilibrium extension is \(4Mg\cdot a/(8Mg)=a/2\). The total potential energy is a quadratic centred at \(a/2\). Its two equal-energy turning extensions therefore have sum \(a\). One is \(3a/8\), the release extension, so the other is \(5a/8\).

Equivalently, putting the downward displacement equal to \(d\) in the zero-speed energy equation gives \(4Mgd=(4Mg/a)[(3a/8+d)^2-(3a/8)^2]\), whose non-zero root is \(d=a/4\).

Express \(k\) in terms of \(x\) and \(a\).

(b) [4]

Find \(x\).

original.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the original equilibrium the extension is \(x-a\), and Hooke's law gives a tension \(kmg(x-a)/a\). Balance this with the original weight \(2mg\): \[\frac{kmg}{a}(x-a)=2mg.\] Cancelling \(mg\) and rearranging gives \(k=2a/(x-a)\).

Put \(e_0=x-a=2a/k\). The gravitational-energy loss after the load is added is \(5mg(a/2)=5mga/2\). The kinetic energy at the measured position is \(\frac12(5m)(ag/5)=mga/2\). The elastic-energy increase is \[\frac{kmg}{2a}\left((e_0+a/2)^2-e_0^2\right)=mga+\frac{k}{8}mga,\] using \(ke_0/a=2\). Therefore \[\frac52=\frac12+1+\frac{k}{8},\] so \(k=8\), giving \(e_0=a/4\) and \(x=5a/4\).

The next stopping descent would be \(3a/4\), so the measured descent \(a/2\) is reached with positive speed before that stop.

original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(m\) rests on a rough horizontal table and is joined to a fixed point \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(3mg\). original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) rests on a rough horizontal table and is joined to a fixed point \(A\) by a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(3mg\). It is held at \(AP=3a/2\), then released from rest. The coefficient of friction is \(\mu\), used both for sliding friction and for the limiting value of static friction.

(a) [3]

Find the range of \(\mu\) for which the particle starts moving but the string never becomes slack.

(b) [3]

For \(\mu=1\), find the extension at the first stop and determine whether the particle remains there.
original.hint_html: A zero speed is not by itself proof of permanent rest. Compare the remaining tension with the maximum available static friction.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Initially the tension is \(3mg/2\), so motion starts only if \(\mu\lt3/2\). Initially the elastic energy is \(3mga/8\). To reach natural length the particle must travel \(a/2\) against friction, requiring work \(\mu mga/2\). It reaches natural length with no positive speed precisely when \(\mu\geq3/4\).

For \(3/4\leq\mu\lt3/2\), the first stopping extension obtained from energy is \(e_1=2\mu a/3-a/2\). Its tension is \((2\mu-3/2)mg\leq\mu mg\), so static friction can hold it. At \(\mu=3/4\), it stops exactly at natural length without passing into a slack interval.

Part (b)

If the final extension is \(e\), the distance travelled is \(a/2-e\). Work and energy give \[\frac38mga=\frac{3mg}{2a}e^2+mg\left(\frac a2-e\right).\] The roots are \(e=a/2\), the initial position, and \(e=a/6\), the first later stop. The tension there is \(mg/2\), below the available static-friction limit \(mg\). Static friction adjusts to \(mg/2\) away from \(A\), and the particle stays at rest.

original.stem_html: A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(mg\). The other end is fixed at \(O\) on a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\). The particle is released from rest at \(O\) and moves down a line of greatest slope. original.question_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a light elastic string of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(mg\). The other end is fixed at \(O\) on a rough plane inclined at \(30^\circ\). The particle is released from rest at \(O\) and moves down a line of greatest slope. The magnitude of sliding friction is \(31mg/80\); the maximum available static friction is the same. The string does not obstruct the motion while slack.

(a) [5]

Find the distance travelled before the particle first comes to rest.

(b) [3]

Determine the magnitude and direction of friction needed to keep the particle at rest there, and decide whether rest is possible.
original.hint_html: Work is done against friction even before the string becomes taut. At the final position, find the required static friction afresh.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(8a/5\).

(b)

\(mg/10\) down the plane; rest is possible.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

The net work per unit distance from gravity and sliding friction is \[mg\sin30^\circ-\frac{31}{80}mg=\frac9{80}mg.\] This is positive, so the particle moves through the initial slack interval. If the later extension is \(e\), the total distance travelled is \(a+e\), not \(e\). At the first stop, \[\frac{mg}{2a}e^2=\frac9{80}mg(a+e).\] Writing \(z=e/a\) gives \(40z^2-9z-9=0=(5z-3)(8z+3)\). The physical root is \(z=3/5\), so the total distance is \(8a/5\).

During the taut phase the kinetic energy is \(mga[9(1+z)/80-z^2/2]\), positive for \(0\leq z\lt3/5\); the root found is the first stop.

Part (b)

At the stop the tension is \(mg(3a/5)/a=3mg/5\) uphill. The downhill weight component is \(mg/2\). Therefore a downhill frictional force of \[\frac35mg-\frac12mg=\frac1{10}mg\] is needed for equilibrium. This is less than \(31mg/80\), so it is available and the particle can remain at rest. Static friction is not automatically equal to its limiting value, and its direction here is opposite to its direction during the descent.

original.stem_html: A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(12mg\) has its lower end fixed on a horizontal plane. A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its upper end. original.question_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(12mg\) has its lower end fixed on a horizontal plane. A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its upper end. Find the greatest extension above natural length.

(b) [1]

Find the acceleration immediately after release.
original.hint_html: Compression stores positive elastic energy. Its force is upwards here, while extension would make the spring pull down.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(x\) be signed extension, positive upwards from natural length. Total potential energy, apart from a constant, is \[U(x)=\frac{6mg}{a}x^2+mgx.\] Initially \(x=-a/2\), so \(U=mga\). At the upper turning point set \(x=za\) and \(K=0\): \[6z^2+z=1,\qquad (3z-1)(2z+1)=0.\] The root \(z=-1/2\) is the release point. The other root is \(z=1/3\), hence the greatest extension is \(a/3\).

Part (b)

The compressed spring pushes upwards with force \(12mg(a/2)/a=6mg\). After subtracting the weight, the resultant is \(5mg\) upwards, so the acceleration is \(5g\).

At equilibrium the extension is \(a\), so the equilibrium distance below \(O\) is \(4a\). The release length is \(4a+d\) and its extension is \(a+d\).

While rising at a height \(3a/2\) above \(O\), the particle has speed \(\sqrt{11ag/2}\) and acceleration \(4g\) downwards. The idealised fixed end does not obstruct the launch.

Find \(\lambda\).

(b) [2]

Find the launch speed.

(c) [4]

original.hint_html: The string pulls down when the particle is above O. Its elastic energy is zero throughout the initial slack interval.

Part (a)

At height \(3a/2\), the extension is \(a/2\). Both tension and weight act downwards, so \(T+mg=4mg\), giving \(T=3mg\). Since \(T=\lambda(a/2)/a=\lambda/2\), the modulus is \(\lambda=6mg\).

Part (b)

At the measured position, kinetic energy is \(11mga/4\), gravitational energy above \(O\) is \(3mga/2\), and elastic energy is \(\frac{6mg}{2a}(a/2)^2=3mga/4\). Their sum is \(5mga\). At launch the string has zero elastic energy, so \(\frac12mu^2=5mga\), giving \(u=\sqrt{10ag}\).

The greatest height is beyond the measured point, so the string is taut there. Write the height as \(a(1+z)\), with \(z\gt1/2\). At the upper turning point kinetic energy is zero, so \[mga(1+z)+3mga z^2=5mga.\] Thus \(3z^2+z-4=0=(3z+4)(z-1)\). Only \(z=1\) is physically admissible, yielding height \(2a\). During the ascent the acceleration is always downward, both in the slack phase and after tension starts, so this is the unique upper turning point.

Fixed points \(A\) and \(B\) are at the same level and \(6a\) apart. A uniform light elastic string of natural length \(6a\) and modulus \(\lambda\) has its ends attached to \(A\) and \(B\). A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to its midpoint. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). In equilibrium the particle is \(4a\) vertically below \(M\). Each half of the string has natural length \(3a\) and the same modulus \(\lambda\).

(a) [3]

Find \(\lambda\).

(b) [4]

The particle is pulled down to \(36a/5\) below \(M\) and released from rest. Show that it reaches \(M\) with zero speed. Explain why it does not stop earlier.
original.hint_html: Use the energy of both half-strings. Equal initial and final total energies are not sufficient unless the intermediate path is accessible.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(\lambda=15mg/16\).

(b)

It first stops at \(M\), with speed zero.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

At equilibrium each half has length \(\sqrt{(3a)^2+(4a)^2}=5a\), hence extension \(2a\). Each tension is \(T=2\lambda/3\). The vertical component of each tension is \(4T/5\), so \[2\left(\frac{4T}{5}\right)=mg.\] Thus \(T=5mg/8\), and \(\lambda=(3/2)T=15mg/16\). The modulus is not halved when a uniform string is divided into halves.

Part (b)

At release each half has length \[\sqrt{9a^2+\frac{1296}{25}a^2}=\frac{39a}{5},\] so each extension is \(24a/5\). The total elastic energy is \[2\frac{\lambda(24a/5)^2}{2(3a)}=\frac{36}{5}mga.\] At \(M\) the string is at natural length and this energy is exactly the gravitational gain \(36mga/5\). Hence the speed at \(M\) is zero.

For a downward separation \(h\), the upward elastic resultant is \[\frac{2\lambda}{3a}\left(h-\frac{3ah}{\sqrt{9a^2+h^2}}\right).\] It increases strictly with \(h\gt0\) and equals \(mg\) only at \(h=4a\). Thus the total potential energy has its unique minimum there: it decreases from the release position to equilibrium and then increases to its value at \(M\). It is strictly below the release energy at every intermediate point, so there is no earlier stop. At \(M\), gravity acts downwards and the particle reverses direction.

original.question_html:
A particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) is attached to a light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(6mg\), whose other end is fixed at \(O\) on a smooth horizontal table. Initially \(P\) is at rest and the spring is at natural length. A second particle \(Q\), of mass \(km\), approaches \(P\) along the spring line towards \(O\), at speed \(2\sqrt{ag}\). They collide and stick together. The greatest compression reached subsequently is \(a/3\). The spring is kept straight.

(a) [4]

Find \(k\).

(b) [2]

Find the kinetic energy lost in the collision.
original.hint_html: Use momentum for the impact, then energy for the subsequent compression. Do not conserve mechanical energy across a sticking collision.
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

During the short collision the elastic force has no appreciable impulse. If the common speed immediately afterwards is \(U\), conservation of momentum gives \[km(2\sqrt{ag})=(1+k)mU,\qquad U=\frac{2k}{1+k}\sqrt{ag}.\] Kinetic energy is not conserved in this sticking collision. It is conserved with elastic potential energy in the subsequent smooth motion: \[\frac12(1+k)mU^2=\frac{6mg}{2a}\left(\frac a3\right)^2=\frac13mga.\] Substitution gives \(6k^2=1+k\), or \((3k+1)(2k-1)=0\). Since the mass is positive, \(k=1/2\).

Part (b)

Initially the kinetic energy is \(\frac12(\frac12m)(2\sqrt{ag})^2=mga\). Immediately after the collision it is \(mga/3\), equal to the later maximum elastic energy. Therefore the collision loss is \(mga-mga/3=2mga/3\).

original.title: An impact, a smooth section and the edge of a rough strip
original.stem_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(6mg\) has one end fixed at \(O\) on a horizontal table and the other attached to a particle \(A\) of mass \(km\). Initially it is at natural length and \(A\) is at rest. A particle \(B\) of mass \(m\) strikes \(A\) directly towards \(O\) with speed \(\sqrt{3ag/2}\); the particles stick together. The spring remains straight.

The motion is smooth until the combined particle reaches \(C\), where the spring length is \(3a/4\). Immediately before reaching \(C\) its speed is half the speed immediately after the collision. At \(C\) it enters a rough strip on the side nearer \(O\), with coefficient of sliding friction \(\mu\). There is no impact or step at the boundary. Immediately after entering the strip its deceleration is \(3g/4\).
original.question_html:
A light spring of natural length \(a\) and modulus \(6mg\) has one end fixed at \(O\) on a horizontal table and the other attached to a particle \(A\) of mass \(km\). Initially it is at natural length and \(A\) is at rest. A particle \(B\) of mass \(m\) strikes \(A\) directly towards \(O\) with speed \(\sqrt{3ag/2}\); the particles stick together. The spring remains straight.

The motion is smooth until the combined particle reaches \(C\), where the spring length is \(3a/4\). Immediately before reaching \(C\) its speed is half the speed immediately after the collision. At \(C\) it enters a rough strip on the side nearer \(O\), with coefficient of sliding friction \(\mu\). There is no impact or step at the boundary. Immediately after entering the strip its deceleration is \(3g/4\).

(a) [6]

Find \(k\).

(b) [4]

Find \(\mu\), explaining what happens to the speed and acceleration at the boundary of the strip.
original.hint_html: At C the spring is compressed, so its force and friction act in the same direction. Neither an energy loss nor a speed jump occurs at a zero-width boundary without an impulse.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=2\).

(b)

\(\mu=1/4\). Speed is continuous; the deceleration changes from \(g/2\) to \(3g/4\).
original.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(u=\sqrt{3ag/2}\), and let \(U\) be the common speed after collision. Momentum gives \(mu=(k+1)mU\), so \(U=u/(k+1)\).

Before the rough strip, the compression at \(C\) is \(a/4\). Energy lost from the combined particle's motion is stored in the spring: \[\frac12(k+1)m\left(U^2-\frac{U^2}{4}\right)=\frac{6mg}{2a}\left(\frac a4\right)^2=\frac3{16}mga.\] Substituting \(U^2=3ag/[2(k+1)^2]\) gives \(9/[16(k+1)]=3/16\). Hence \(k+1=3\), and \(k=2\). The common speed at \(C\) is \(u/6\).

Part (b)

At \(C\), the spring pushes away from \(O\) with force \(6mg(a/4)/a=3mg/2\). The combined mass is \(3m\), so immediately before the boundary the deceleration is \(g/2\).

After entry, friction \(3\mu mg\) also acts away from \(O\), opposing the motion. Hence \[\frac32mg+3\mu mg=3m\frac{3g}{4},\] which gives \(\mu=1/4\). There is no impulsive force at the boundary, so the speed cannot jump. The force, and therefore the acceleration, changes discontinuously as friction starts to act.
